content: 1. Trazodone: The levels of trazodone may be increased through an unspecified interaction mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 2. Sulfamethoxazole and Triamterene: Sulfamethoxazole increases the levels or effects of triamterene due to competition for renal tubular clearance of basic (cationic) drugs. Similarly, triamterene increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. 3. Sulfamethoxazole and Trimethoprim: Sulfamethoxazole increases the levels or effects of trimethoprim via competition for renal tubular clearance of basic drugs. The clinical significance is unknown. 4. Sulfamethoxazole and Trimipramine: Sulfamethoxazole decreases the levels of trimipramine through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown. 5. Valganciclovir and Sulfamethoxazole: Valganciclovir increases the toxicity of sulfamethoxazole through pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance is unknown. 6. Valproic Acid and Sulfamethoxazole: Valproic acid increases the levels or effects of sulfamethoxazole by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown. 7. Sulfamethoxazole and Verapamil: Sulfamethoxazole increases the levels or effects of verapamil through competition for renal tubular clearance of basic drugs. Trimethoprim also increases verapamil levels via the same mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown. 8. Sulfamethoxazole and Verteporfin: Sulfamethoxazole increases phototoxicity when combined with verteporfin due to pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance is unknown. 9. Sulfamethoxazole and Voriconazole: Sulfamethoxazole increases the levels or effects of voriconazole by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. Voriconazole similarly increases sulfamethoxazole levels. The clinical significance is unknown. 10. Willow Bark and Sulfamethoxazole: Willow bark increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown. 11. Zafirlukast and Sulfamethoxazole: Zafirlukast increases the levels or effects of sulfamethoxazole by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown. 12. Zidovudine and Sulfamethoxazole: Zidovudine increases the toxicity of sulfamethoxazole through pharmacodynamic synergism. Sulfamethoxazole increases zidovudine levels by decreasing renal clearance. The clinical significance is unknown. 13. Acetazolamide and Trimethoprim: Acetazolamide increases the levels or effects of trimethoprim by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown. 14. Trimethoprim and Aliskiren: Both drugs increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim decreases urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia, especially at high doses, in renal insufficiency, or when combined with other hyperkalemia-inducing drugs. Use caution and monitor closely. 15. Sulfamethoxazole and Alosetron: Sulfamethoxazole increases the levels or effects of alosetron by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown. 16. Alpelisib and Trimethoprim: Alpelisib decreases the levels or effects of trimethoprim by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. Therapy modification or close monitoring is recommended. 17. Trimethoprim and Amantadine: Trimethoprim increases amantadine levels by decreasing elimination. Sulfamethoxazole similarly increases amantadine levels. Co-administration may impair renal clearance of amantadine, leading to higher plasma concentrations. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Trimethoprim and Amiloride: Both drugs increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim decreases urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia, particularly at high doses, in renal insufficiency, or when combined with other hyperkalemia-inducing drugs. Use caution and monitor closely. 19. Amiloride and Sulfamethoxazole: Amiloride increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown. 20. Aminobenzoate Potassium and Sulfamethoxazole: Aminobenzoate potassium decreases the effects of sulfamethoxazole through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 21. Sulfamethoxazole and Aminohippurate Sodium: Sulfamethoxazole interferes with the chemical color development of aminohippurate (PAH), which is essential for accurate renal clearance analysis. The clinical significance is unknown. 22. Aminolevulinic Acid (Oral) and Sulfamethoxazole: Both drugs increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Avoid administering other phototoxic drugs with aminolevulinic acid oral for 24 hours during the perioperative period. 23. Aminolevulinic Acid (Topical) and Sulfamethoxazole: Both drugs increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially enhancing photosensitizing effects. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 24. Amiodarone and Sulfamethoxazole: Amiodarone increases sulfamethoxazole levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. Both drugs increase the QTc interval. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 25. Amitriptyline and Sulfamethoxazole: Both drugs increase the QTc interval. Sulfamethoxazole decreases amitriptyline levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown. 26. Amobarbital and Sulfamethoxazole: Amobarbital decreases sulfamethoxazole levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown. 27. Amoxapine and Sulfamethoxazole: Both drugs increase the QTc interval. Sulfamethoxazole decreases amoxapine levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown. 28. Anastrozole and Trimethoprim: Anastrozole increases trimethoprim levels by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown. 29. Sulfamethoxazole and Antithrombin Alfa/III: Sulfamethoxazole increases the effects of antithrombin alfa and antithrombin III by decreasing metabolism and through plasma protein binding competition. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 30. Apalutamide and Trimethoprim: Apalutamide decreases trimethoprim levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 and CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 31. Sulfamethoxazole and Argatroban: Sulfamethoxazole increases the effects of argatroban by decreasing metabolism and through plasma protein binding competition. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 32. Sulfamethoxazole and Artemether/Lumefantrine: Both drugs increase the QTc interval. Modify therapy or monitor closely. 33. Sulfamethoxazole and Aspirin: Both drugs may increase each other's effects through plasma protein binding competition. Use caution and monitor closely. 34. Sulfamethoxazole and Azathioprine: Sulfamethoxazole may cause leukopenia due to additive myelosuppression when combined with azathioprine. The clinical significance is unknown. 35. Sulfamethoxazole and Azithromycin: Both drugs increase the QTc interval. The clinical significance is unknown. 36. Trimethoprim and Balsalazide: Trimethoprim decreases balsalazide levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. 37. Sulfamethoxazole and BCG Vaccine (Live): Sulfamethoxazole decreases the effects of the BCG vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Administration of live bacterial vaccines should be delayed until antibiotic therapy is complete. 38. Sulfamethoxazole and Bemiparin: Sulfamethoxazole increases the effects of bemiparin by decreasing metabolism and through plasma protein binding competition. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 39. Trimethoprim and Benazepril: Both drugs increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim decreases urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia. Use caution and monitor closely. 40. Sulfamethoxazole and Biotin: Sulfamethoxazole decreases biotin levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. 41. Sulfamethoxazole and Bivalirudin: Sulfamethoxazole increases the effects of bivalirudin by decreasing metabolism and through plasma protein binding competition. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 42. Sulfamethoxazole and Bosentan: Sulfamethoxazole increases bosentan levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown. 43. Sulfamethoxazole and Bumetanide: Bumetanide increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown. 44. Sulfamethoxazole and Butabarbital: Butabarbital decreases sulfamethoxazole levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown. 45. Trimethoprim and Canagliflozin: Both drugs increase serum potassium levels. Use caution and monitor closely. 46. Trimethoprim and Candesartan: Both drugs increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim decreases urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia. Use caution and monitor closely. 47. Sulfamethoxazole and Cannabidiol: Cannabidiol increases trimethoprim levels by decreasing metabolism. Consider reducing the dose of trimethoprim when co-administered. 48. Trimethoprim and Captopril: Both drugs increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim decreases urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia. Use caution and monitor closely. 49. Sulfamethoxazole and Carbamazepine: Carbamazepine decreases sulfamethoxazole levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown. 50. Sulfamethoxazole and Carvedilol: Sulfamethoxazole increases carvedilol levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. This list continues with similar detailed interactions for other drugs.
